extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of social science, political economy, and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on methods for constructing and verifying social-scientific theories: when to use deductive (hypothetical) abstractions versus historical/inductive inquiry, how to delimit branches like political economy, and how to use empirical verification and statistics. Emphasizes limits of abstraction, role of national character (ethology), and standards for applying theory across societies and times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical/deductive propositions are conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: The propositions of deductive science are, in the strictest sense of the word, hypothetical. They are grounded on some suppositious set of circumstances, and declare how some given cause would operate in those circumstances, supposing that no others were combined with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conclusions are true of an existing society only 'provided, and in as far as, the effect of those circumstances shall not be modified by others which have not been taken into the account.' To approach concrete truth, include more individualizing circumstances, but beware that adding many concurrent causes rapidly increases uncertainty and liability to error; therefore limit hypothetical deductions to classes of social facts chiefly influenced by a few causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit complexity of causal combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing general theorems, hypothetical combinations of circumstances cannot be made very complex without quickly accumulating liability to error that will deprive conclusions of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On pain of frivolity, limit deductive inquiry to social facts under the immediate influence principally of a few causes. If a nearer approach to concrete truth is desired, increase particulars only cautiously, recognizing rapidly increasing uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate branches when immediate causes differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Different species of social facts are in the main dependent, immediately and in the first resort, on different kinds of causes; and therefore not only may with advantage, but must, be studied apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create distinct (though not independent) departments of sociological speculation—analogous to studying different organs in physiology—while remaining mindful of the universal consensus by which each part influences the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and abstraction of Political Economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Political Economy concerns itself only with 'such of the phenomena of the social state as take place in consequence of the pursuit of wealth.' It makes entire abstraction of every other human passion or motive except aversion to labor and desire of present enjoyment (treated as antagonistic drags).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the main and acknowledged end (acquisition/consumption of wealth) as if it were the sole end for analytic tractability, then later correct for other impulses. Use the simplified hypothesis to derive laws (rent, profit, wages) under free competition, then adjust when applying to real societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat theoretical conclusions as conditional on premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusions of abstract sciences are asserted only conditionally, subject to the control of the general science; their applicability depends on whether the premises (social circumstances) match the target society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying conclusions to another society, trace back demonstrations and introduce new premises where appropriate. Be wary of extrapolating from the particulars of one state of society (e.g., England) to dissimilar societies without revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check premises when applying theory across societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Many political-economical conclusions are adapted to a society constituted in particular ways (e.g., three distinct classes: laborers, capitalists, landlords); they require revision whenever applied to societies with different structures (e.g., slave countries, state-landlord systems, different land/capital ownership patterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify structural differences (ownership, freedom of agents, class separations) and revise the theory's premises accordingly; failure to do so is a common error of political economists who treat local arrangements as immutable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of political ethology (national character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political Ethology (theory of causes determining the type of character belonging to a people or age) is a comprehensive branch whose laws strongly influence other sociological branches but is still in infancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study national/collective character because it largely determines and is determined by institutions, customs, laws, government form, and the character of governors. Recognize that many abstract conclusions must be modified by ethological considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate ethological influences where inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Some social phenomena are so mixed up with the ethological state of the people that 'the connection of effects and causes cannot be even rudely marked out without taking those influences into consideration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where ethological influences are pervasive (e.g., questions of forms of government), these matters cannot advantageously be treated as separate sciences; they must be part of the general science of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical/statistical generalizations as preparatory data
rubrics_metrics.description: In statistics, empirical laws may sometimes be traced and collecting such approximate generalizations forms an important part of the indirect observation on which deductive science must often rely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When causes are not directly observable, infer them from effects via statistical empirical laws—but remember these are approximations and must be used with knowledge of remoter causes that determine when the empirical law applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of empirical laws (approximate and contingent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws obtained by observation are never more than approximate generalizations and can only be relied on for new cases so long as there is reason to think no change has taken place in any of the remote causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying empirical generalizations to cases differing in remoter causes. Always refer empirical inferences to deductive theory to check applicability; the deductive science should 'stand sentinel' over the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific experience often cannot verify single-cause effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In many special inquiries (e.g., effect of corn laws), the object is to determine the effect of one social cause among many simultaneous ones; specific experience cannot furnish empirical laws here because effects are disguised by other influencing agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the number of instances needed to average out combinations of circumstances is unattainable; direct experimental verification is usually impossible since no two social cases share exactly the same circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct verification of theory by single experiments is generally impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: To verify a theory by an experiment, the experiment's circumstances must match theory's assumptions exactly; social circumstances of no two cases are exactly alike, so the only truly fitting instance is the case for which the prediction was originally made (verification comes too late for guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-reliance on single historical trials as proofs; treat such individual verifications as of limited practical use for prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of indirect verification via multiple instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Although direct verification is often impossible, there is an indirect verification: the conclusion about an individual case is indirectly verified by verifying other conclusions drawn in other individual cases from the same laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test a theory by its capacity to explain multiple past instances; the test of a science's predictive ground is the degree to which it would have enabled us to predict what has actually occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for predictive competence: explain past and present
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that our science renders us competent to predict the future, we must show that it would have enabled us to predict the present and the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anything in the present or past could not have been predicted by the theory, treat it as a residual phenomenon requiring further search among case-specific circumstances or an extension/improvement of the theory itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and components of a 'state of society'
rubrics_metrics.description: A state of society is the simultaneous state of all the greater social facts: degree of knowledge and culture, state of industry, wealth and its distribution, habitual occupations, class divisions and relations, common beliefs, tastes and aesthetic development, form of government, important laws and customs, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing societies, consider the natural correlation (uniformities of co-existence) among these elements; only certain combinations are possible because each element influences the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental problem: laws of succession (progressiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental problem of social science is to find the laws according to which any state of society produces the state which succeeds it and takes its place—the laws of succession and co-existence of great social facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between cyclical (orbit) and progressive (trajectory) models; the method should aim to detect regularities of succession, but be cautious about conflating empirical historical order with laws of nature—the latter requires connection to causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progressiveness is methodological, not automatically improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress and progressiveness signify change from age to age (not necessarily improvement); the method presumes progressive change in character and circumstances of the human race and society across generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical/trajectory analysis to identify patterns of succession; recognize that 'progress' as a methodological presupposition does not imply moral or intrinsic improvement without further argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical method yields empirical law, requires causal grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting by analysis of general facts of history to discover a law of progress can produce an empirical law, but such an order of succession 'can only be an empirical law' unless connected with psychological and ethological laws from which it derives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat historical uniformities of succession as natural laws without linking them to the underlying causal laws (psychological/ethological) that truly determine them; combine historical induction with causal explanation.
